---
title: "The Hangover Effects of COVID-19 for New York City"
format:
    html:
        output-file: "index.html"
---

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(reactable)
library(ggplot2)
library(crosstalk)
```

On January 31st, 2020, The Untied States declared a public health emergency 
for the corona virus: COVID-19. During which over 1.2 million Americans died.
The pandemic officially ended on May 11th, 2023. However, for New York City 
the impacts of COVID-19 did not end at the same time. The effects that
COVID-19 has had on the city can be seen in the numbers of residents on SNAP,
cash assistance, and Medicaid.

New York City is split into 5 boroughs, with each further split into many
community districts. The dataset gave the number of residents on each of
SNAP, cash assistance, and Medicaid. This information was updated each
quarter on the first day of the month for March, June, September, and December.

To analyze this data I grouped the entries by borough then averaged over the
community districts.

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Link to the dataset
# https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Social-Services/Cash-Assistance-Medicaid-and-SNAP-Borough-Communit/5awp-wfkt/about_data
file <- "Cash_Assistance,_Medicaid,_and_SNAP_-_Borough_Community_District_Report_20261103.csv"
data <- read.csv(file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE);

# Convert number string into number. e.g. "1,234" into 1234
numericCols <- 4:9
data[,numericCols] <- lapply(data[,numericCols],function(x){as.numeric(gsub(",", "", x))})
# Merge names "Staten_Island" and "Staten Island"
data <- data |> mutate(Borough = if_else(Borough == "Staten_Island", "Staten Island", Borough))
# Convert date string to date object for graphing
data <- data |> mutate(Month = as.POSIXct(Month, format="%m/%d/%Y"))

# Important dates to graph later
COVID_start <- as.POSIXct("1/31/2020", format="%m/%d/%Y")
COVID_end <- as.POSIXct("5/11/2023", format="%m/%d/%Y")
```

```{r}
snap <- data |>
    summarize(mean_SNAP = mean(Borough.Consultation.Total.SNAP.Recipients), .by = c(Borough, Month))

p <- ggplot(snap) +
    aes(x = Month, y = mean_SNAP, color = Borough) + 
    geom_point()

p <- p + labs(title = "Avg. number of Residents on SNAP by Borough", x = "Quarter", y = "")

top <- 40000
bottom <- 15000
text_height <- 37500

p <- p + annotate("segment", x = COVID_start, y = bottom, xend = COVID_start, yend = top, color = "red", lty = "dotted")
p <- p + annotate("segment", x = COVID_end, y = bottom, xend = COVID_end, yend = top, color = "green", lty = "dotted")
p <- p + annotate("text", x=COVID_start, y=text_height, label="COVID-19 begins", hjust=-0.1, color="red",family="sans")
p <- p + annotate("text", x=COVID_end, y=text_height, label="COVID-19 ends", hjust=-0.1, color="green",family="sans")

p  
```

Here we see the average number of residents on SNAP assistance grouped by borough.
By visual inspection we see for the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Manhattan the number of residents on
SNAP has only recently, since 2026, dipped below pre-COVID levels. For the Queens
and Staten Island, they have yet to fully recover.

```{r}
medicaid <- data |>
    summarize(mean_MAID = mean(Borough.Consultation.Total.Medicaid.Enrollees), .by = c(Borough, Month))

top <- 40000
bottom <- 15000
text_height <- 37500

p <- ggplot(medicaid) +
    aes(x = Month, y = mean_MAID, color = Borough) + 
    geom_point() +
    ylim(bottom, top)

p <- p + labs(title = "Avg. number of Residents on Medicaid by Borough", x = "Quarter", y = "")

p <- p + annotate("segment", x = COVID_start, y = bottom, xend = COVID_start, yend = top, color = "red", lty = "dotted")
p <- p + annotate("segment", x = COVID_end, y = bottom, xend = COVID_end, yend = top, color = "green", lty = "dotted")
p <- p + annotate("text", x=COVID_start, y=text_height, label="COVID-19 begins", hjust=-0.1, color="red",family="sans")
p <- p + annotate("text", x=COVID_end, y=text_height, label="COVID-19 ends", hjust=-0.1, color="green",family="sans")

p  
```
The Medicaid numbers tell a difference story. The numbers for all boroughs kept
constant and actually increased after the official end of COVID. This could be
because of the success that COVID-era stimulus had on keeping people financially
afloat so as to not be eligible for Medicaid. But after COVID this stimulus ended. So 
those who did not completely recover may have fell into poverty and thus being 
eligible for Medicaid.

```{r}
cash <- data |>
    summarize(mean_cash = mean(Borough.Consultation.Total.Cash.Assistance.Recipients), .by = c(Borough, Month))

p <- ggplot(cash) +
    aes(x = Month, y = mean_cash, color = Borough) + 
    geom_point()

p <- p + labs(title = "Avg. number of Residents on Cash Assistance by Borough", x = "Quarter", y = "")

top <- 20000
bottom <- 2500
text_height <- 18000

p <- p + annotate("segment", x = COVID_start, y = bottom, xend = COVID_start, yend = top, color = "red", lty = "dotted")
p <- p + annotate("segment", x = COVID_end, y = bottom, xend = COVID_end, yend = top, color = "green", lty = "dotted")
p <- p + annotate("text", x=COVID_start, y=text_height, label="COVID-19 begins", hjust=-0.1, color="red",family="sans")
p <- p + annotate("text", x=COVID_end, y=text_height, label="COVID-19 ends", hjust=-0.1, color="green",family="sans")

p  
```
There was an increasing number of residences on cash assistance from the end of
2021 to mid 2025. The Bronx saw the largest increase with the other four following
a similar, but less intense, pattern. This is most likely due to the long-term
disruptions COVID had on the economy.

In conclusion, while COVID-19 officially ended over three years ago. The city of New
York is still addressing the needs of those affected by COVID to this day.
